```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(patchwork)
library(broom)

penguins2 <- penguins |>
  select(species, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) |>
  drop_na()

overall_mod <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins2)
species_mod <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm + species, data = penguins2)

overall_r <- cor(penguins2$bill_length_mm, penguins2$bill_depth_mm)
by_species_r <- penguins2 |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(r = cor(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm), n = n())
```

## Introduction

- Penguin bill length and bill depth are both used to distinguish species and assess body condition in the Palmer Archipelago penguins studied by @gorman2014ecological.
- A researcher who pools all species together and fits a single regression line would conclude that longer bills go with *shallower* bills -- a negative relationship.
- That pooled conclusion reverses once species is accounted for. This is a textbook case of **Simpson's paradox**: ignoring a grouping variable (species) can flip the sign of an association.

## Data

- **Source:** `palmerpenguins` R package [@horst2020palmerpenguins], based on data collected at Palmer Station, Antarctica [@gorman2014ecological].
- **Sample:** `r nrow(penguins)` penguins measured; `r nrow(penguins2)` have complete bill measurements and are used below.
- **Species counts:** `r by_species_r$n[1]` Adelie, `r by_species_r$n[2]` Chinstrap, `r by_species_r$n[3]` Gentoo.

## Approach

- Fit a simple linear regression of bill depth on bill length **pooling all species together**.
- Fit a second regression that **adds species as a covariate**, so each species gets its own intercept but a shared slope.
- Compare the sign and size of the bill-length slope between the two models, and check the within-species correlations directly.
- All modeling was conducted in R [@rcore2026] using the tidyverse [@tidyverse2019] and ggplot2 [@ggplot22016]; model summaries were tidied with broom [@broom2026], the figure below was composed with patchwork [@patchwork2025], and tables were typeset with knitr [@knitr2025].

## Results

The pooled model shows a negative association
(Pearson's *r* = `r round(overall_r, 2)`), while every species shows a
*positive* within-species correlation (@tbl-by-species). Adjusting for
species reverses the sign of the slope entirely (@fig-simpson,
@tbl-coefs).

```{r}
#| label: fig-simpson
#| fig-cap: "Pooling across species (left) suggests bill depth decreases with bill length. Looking within each species (right) shows the opposite: bill depth increases with bill length in every species."
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 8
p_pooled <- ggplot(penguins2, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#666666", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#A8384F") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)",
       title = "All species pooled") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_species <- ggplot(penguins2, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0047B3", "#CC0033", "#00205B")) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)",
       title = "Same data, by species", color = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p_pooled / p_species
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-by-species
#| tbl-cap: "Within-species correlation between bill length and bill depth is positive for all three species."
#| echo: false
by_species_r |>
  mutate(r = round(r, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Species", "Correlation (r)", "n"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusting for species (model 2) reverses the sign of the bill-length coefficient compared to the pooled model (model 1)."
#| echo: false
bind_rows(
  tidy(overall_mod) |> mutate(model = "1: Pooled"),
  tidy(species_mod) |> mutate(model = "2: + Species")
) |>
  filter(term == "bill_length_mm") |>
  transmute(Model = model, Term = "Bill length (mm)",
            Estimate = round(estimate, 3), `Std. Error` = round(std.error, 3),
            `p-value` = signif(p.value, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Conclusions and Next Steps

- A relationship estimated from pooled data can have the **opposite
  sign** of the relationship within each subgroup -- always check
  whether a natural grouping variable is confounding an association
  before reporting a pooled effect.
- Next steps: extend the species-adjusted model to test for
  differing slopes by species (an interaction), and consider sex and
  island as additional covariates.
